label: Intellectual Developmental Disorder
name: Avery Rowan
strengths: Enjoys making models, remembers practical routines and explains ideas well with pictures.
needs: Needs concrete examples, short directions and supported practice to organize a multi-step task. Written output does not always show understanding.
goal_action: use a picture checklist to complete a three-step classroom task with no more than one adult prompt
support: Provide a three-step picture checklist with a worked example during independent tasks.
proposal: Provide the picture checklist before independent tasks in both courses; model the first example and record independent versus prompted steps separately.
observation_a: A picture checklist was available for all five practical tasks; the student completed three tasks with one prompt or fewer.
observation_b: The checklist was available in only two of five written tasks. In the other tasks, multiple oral reminders were used; effectiveness without the checklist cannot be judged.
voice: Prefers to check off pictures privately before asking an adult for help.
family: A short checklist helps organize a homework routine; lengthy written directions still need explanation.

label: IDD with tiered support
name: Blake Linden
strengths: Participates in familiar routines, recalls familiar vocabulary and enjoys cooperative art activities.
needs: Benefits from explicit vocabulary teaching and guided practice explaining a choice. Generalization from a supported group to an independent task needs monitoring.
goal_action: use a sentence frame and picture choices to explain a task-related choice in four of five opportunities
support: Offer picture choices and a sentence frame during classroom discussion and supported practice.
proposal: Coordinate universal picture choices, a short small-group rehearsal and individual follow-up; log support level and independent transfer rather than combining all observations.
observation_a: During supported rehearsal, four of five explanations included a reason; adult modeling was recorded for three of those explanations.
observation_b: Only two independent explanations were collected after classroom discussion. Neither included a reason; the small sample does not establish lack of progress.
voice: Would like time to rehearse before sharing an answer with the group.
family: Explains familiar choices at home with pictures; unfamiliar choices still need a sentence starter.

label: Autism Spectrum Disorder
name: Cameron Vale
strengths: Notices patterns, enjoys coding puzzles and contributes detailed ideas in a familiar group.
needs: Needs explicit expectations for group roles, advance notice of changes and a predictable way to request clarification.
goal_action: use a role card to contribute an idea and request clarification during a group task in four of five opportunities
support: Provide a visual agenda and written group-role card before collaborative tasks.
proposal: Provide the agenda and role card before each group task, preview changes privately and offer a written clarification option; collect student feedback about usefulness.
observation_a: With the role card available, the student contributed in four of five planned group tasks and used a written clarification request twice.
observation_b: An unannounced group change occurred in two tasks. The student paused participation and requested an individual explanation; the role card was not updated.
voice: Finds group work easier when the role and any changes are written down before starting.
family: Advance notice of a changed homework routine is useful; the student wants fewer public reminders.

label: ASD with tiered support
name: Devon Ash
strengths: Enjoys sharing interests, builds detailed drawings and readily approaches familiar peers.
needs: Needs supported practice noticing another person's contribution and using predictable turn-taking routines across settings.
interest: Drawing maps and collecting nature facts
goal_action: use a visual turn-taking cue to ask a peer a relevant question and allow a response in four of five observed exchanges
support: Use a visual turn-taking cue and a brief rehearsal before paired tasks.
proposal: Use the same cue across class routines, small-group rehearsal and individual coaching; record the support level and allow the student to choose a discreet cue.
observation_a: Four of five rehearsed exchanges included a peer question with the cue visible; two required an adult reminder.
observation_b: During a less structured activity, the cue was not available and only one exchange was recorded. Transfer to that setting remains uncertain.
voice: Prefers a small desk cue to a teacher pointing to a large class chart.
family: Practice with a familiar adult is comfortable, but the family requests gradual practice with peers.

label: Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
name: Ellis Brook
strengths: Asks thoughtful questions, generates creative solutions and participates enthusiastically in hands-on work.
needs: Needs support starting, sequencing and checking independent work. Longer uninterrupted tasks are harder to sustain than short tasks with clear checkpoints.
goal_action: use a short task plan and a planned break to complete and check three work segments in four of five sessions
support: Break independent work into short segments and offer a planned movement break.
proposal: Agree on segment length with the student, offer a discreet break prompt and a return-to-task cue, and log whether each support was actually available before rating helpfulness.
observation_a: Three work segments were completed in four of five sessions when a checkpoint and break were offered.
observation_b: Extra time alone was provided in three sessions, without segmenting the task. Completion varied and cannot be attributed to a single support.
voice: Wants a predictable break and a clear first step when returning to work.
family: A short homework plan is easier to follow than an open-ended extra-time allowance.

label: Mental Illness
name: Finley Moss
strengths: Produces thoughtful digital projects, maintains trusted relationships and communicates preferences in writing.
needs: Participation varies with energy and stress. Needs a predictable check-in, manageable workload planning and a way to request support privately; no clinical conclusions are inferred.
goal_action: use an agreed private check-in to identify a manageable next task or request a support in four of five offered opportunities
support: Offer a private check-in, planned rest opportunities and flexible sequencing of independent work.
proposal: Let the student choose a private check-in format, agree on a return-to-learning plan and monitor workload and support availability; do not interpret missing work as a clinical symptom.
observation_a: The student used four of five offered written check-ins to choose a next task and completed the agreed task on three occasions.
observation_b: Two check-ins were missed because of timetable changes. There is insufficient evidence to compare participation on those days.
voice: Prefers a written check-in with a trusted adult and does not want to explain private health information to classmates.
family: Requests predictable communication about workload and flexibility when participation varies.

label: Specific Learning Difficulties in Reading and Writing
name: Gray Marlow
strengths: Explains ideas clearly in discussion, recognizes visual patterns and reasons well about practical problems.
needs: Reading fluency and organizing written responses require support. Access to subject content and practice of reading skills need separate monitoring.
goal_action: use accessible text and a planning organizer to produce a response with a main idea and two relevant details in four of five tasks
support: Provide text-to-speech for subject-content reading and a graphic organizer for written responses.
proposal: Provide accessible text before the task and explicit organizer practice; record content understanding separately from reading fluency, and confirm assessment-specific conditions before testing use.
observation_a: With accessible text and an organizer, four of five responses contained a main idea and two relevant details.
observation_b: Accessible text arrived after the lesson on two occasions. Shorter responses on those tasks do not show whether the planned support was effective.
voice: Wants audio access to content while keeping opportunities to practice reading with instruction.
family: Reports that planning ideas orally before writing reduces frustration during homework.

label: Physical Disability
name: Harper Reed
strengths: Contributes imaginative ideas, remembers story details and collaborates well when materials are accessible.
needs: Physical access and written output need individualized arrangements. Fatigue and input-device availability affect participation without necessarily reflecting content understanding.
goal_action: select an agreed accessible input method and complete a curriculum response in four of five opportunities with setup assistance recorded separately
support: Provide an accessible input device, an alternative response option and planned rest opportunities.
proposal: Check device readiness and workspace access before class; offer the student's preferred response method and record setup assistance and fatigue separately from achievement.
observation_a: The accessible input device was ready for four tasks; the student completed a response in each with setup assistance.
observation_b: The device was unavailable for two tasks. A verbal response was accepted for one; no response opportunity was documented for the other.
voice: Wants classmates to hear the ideas rather than focus on how the response is produced.
family: Requests a consistent backup input option when the usual device is unavailable.

label: Visual Impairment
name: Indigo Lane
strengths: Recalls spoken information, asks precise questions and contributes strong explanations during discussion.
needs: Needs accessible materials before instruction and explicit descriptions of visual information. Format preference and navigation support must be established individually.
goal_action: locate relevant information in an agreed accessible format and explain two key ideas in four of five tasks
support: Provide accessible digital text and agreed magnification or screen-reader access before the lesson.
proposal: Check reading order and image descriptions before sharing materials; confirm the student's preferred format and provide accessible diagrams or an equivalent description before instruction.
observation_a: Accessible text was supplied in advance for five lessons; the student identified key ideas in four tasks.
observation_b: Two diagrams had no accessible description. The student requested clarification, so incomplete diagram responses cannot be treated as a learning deficit.
voice: Prefers materials early enough to check access and asks that diagrams be described during discussion.
family: Reports that consistent file naming and advance access make homework preparation easier.

label: Hearing Impairment
name: Jules Cedar
strengths: Notices visual details, enjoys practical experiments and contributes well when discussion is accessible.
needs: Needs an individually agreed communication-access plan, visible instructions and access to peer contributions. Device use and language preferences must be discussed with the student.
goal_action: use an agreed access or clarification strategy to identify the task and contribute to a discussion in four of five opportunities
support: Provide written key instructions, clear sightlines and one speaker at a time during discussion.
proposal: Add checked captions or equivalent accessible information, repeat peer contributions visibly and agree on a private clarification signal; ask about communication preferences instead of assuming a device or language choice.
observation_a: With written instructions and clear sightlines, the student followed the task in four of five lessons.
observation_b: Captions were missing from two video clips and several peers spoke at once. The student reported missing information despite being seated near the front.
voice: Wants access to classmates' comments and a discreet way to signal that information was missed.
family: Requests accessible instructions for independent work and asks the team to respect communication preferences.

label: Speech and Language Impairment
name: Kai Wren
strengths: Reasons well in mathematics, prepares carefully and shares detailed ideas through drawing and writing.
needs: Needs time and flexible ways to formulate and express a response. Content knowledge should be distinguished from speech fluency and response speed.
goal_action: use a chosen response mode and a planning cue to communicate a main idea and request clarification in four of five tasks
support: Allow planning time, sentence starters and a chosen spoken, written or visual response mode.
proposal: Agree on response mode before discussion, allow unhurried response time without completing the student's sentences, and assess content separately from fluency or speed.
observation_a: With preparation time and a chosen response mode, four of five explanations contained the key idea.
observation_b: Three rapid-response activities did not offer preparation time. Limited spoken responses in those activities do not establish limited understanding.
voice: Wants time to finish an answer and the option to use a prepared visual explanation.
family: Reports that an unhurried listener helps the student explain ideas more fully.

label: Twice Exceptional Student
name: Logan Sage
strengths: Shows advanced reasoning in selected topics, asks original questions and develops ambitious independent projects.
needs: Needs appropriately challenging content alongside explicit planning and collaboration supports. Strong performance in one area does not establish that supports are unnecessary.
interest: Independent scientific investigations and digital media
goal_action: use a project plan and agreed collaboration role to complete a challenging project checkpoint and reflect on support use in four of five opportunities
support: Provide appropriately challenging tasks with a visual project plan and explicit collaboration roles.
proposal: Retain advanced content while adding student-selected planning checkpoints and clear collaboration roles; review challenge level and support access separately rather than removing support because of strong scores.
observation_a: The student completed four advanced-content checkpoints when a visual project plan was available.
observation_b: In a group project with unclear roles, two checkpoints were missed even though the student explained the content accurately.
voice: Wants challenging work and practical planning support without being assigned repetitive replacement tasks.
family: Asks the team to preserve both advanced learning opportunities and individualized supports.
